title: Chole Protein and Calories: The Real Numbers Behind Chana
meta_description: Plain boiled chickpeas have 9g protein at 164 kcal per 100g. Restaurant chole can run double the calories from oil and butter alone. Full breakdown of chole, chana dal, and roasted chana as a snack.
meta_keywords: chole chickpea protein calories, chana protein nutrition, chole calories restaurant vs home, roasted chana protein, chickpea fibre glycaemic index
quick_answer: Plain boiled chickpeas (kabuli chana) have about 9g protein, 164 kcal, and 7.6g fibre per 100g cooked — a solid, low-glycaemic protein source. The chickpeas themselves don't change much between home and restaurant chole; what changes the calorie count dramatically is oil and butter, which can push a restaurant serving to nearly double the calories of a home-cooked one for the same amount of chana.

faq.question: How much protein is in chole?
faq.answer: Plain boiled chickpeas have about 9g protein per 100g cooked. A typical home-style chole serving (chickpeas plus onion-tomato gravy) usually delivers 6–8g protein per 100g, since the gravy adds weight without adding protein. A generous bowl of chole (roughly 200g) still gets you a meaningful 12–16g protein alongside its fibre.

faq.question: Is restaurant chole much higher in calories than home-cooked?
faq.answer: Often yes. Restaurant chole is frequently finished with extra oil, ghee, or a knob of butter for shine and richness, which can add 100–150 kcal per serving over a home-cooked version using 1–2 teaspoons of oil. The chickpeas contribute the same protein either way — the calorie gap is almost entirely about added fat, not the chana itself.

faq.question: Is roasted chana a good high-protein snack?
faq.answer: Yes, and it's more calorie-dense than it looks. Dry roasted chana (roasted whole chickpeas or roasted gram, no oil) has about 19–20g protein per 100g, but also roughly 360–380 kcal per 100g because it's dehydrated rather than cooked in water like chole. A small handful (25–30g) is a reasonable snack portion — treating it like a wet dish and eating a large bowl will add up fast.

intro: Chole chawal and chana chaat are permanent fixtures on Indian plates, but "chana is healthy" gets said without much specificity. The chickpea itself is a genuinely good protein and fibre source — the real variable is what happens to it in the kadhai. Here's the honest breakdown: what plain chana delivers, how much a restaurant's oil and butter change the math, and how roasted chana as a snack compares to chole as a meal.

sections.heading: The baseline: plain boiled chickpeas
sections.body:
Boiled or pressure-cooked kabuli chana (white chickpeas), with no oil or seasoning, delivers approximately 9g protein, 164 kcal, and 7.6g fibre per 100g cooked. That fibre number is genuinely high — more than most dals — which is a big part of why chole is filling in a way that outlasts a plain rice meal.

Chana dal (split Bengal gram, the smaller yellow split lentil used in dal and some sweets) is a different product from whole chickpeas, but similar nutritionally: about 7.3g protein and 164 kcal per 100g cooked, with slightly less fibre at 5.6g. Both are strong everyday protein sources; whole chana edges ahead on fibre, chana dal cooks faster and suits different dishes.

sections.heading: Chole gravy: where the real calorie swing happens
sections.body:
The chickpeas in chole don't lose protein to cooking — moist-heat cooking in gravy doesn't destroy protein, it just gets diluted across a heavier plate once you add onion, tomato, and oil. A home-style chole made with 1–2 teaspoons of oil per serving, standard onion-tomato-spice base, works out to roughly 130–160 kcal and 6–8g protein per 100g including gravy.

Restaurant chole is a different story. To get the glossy, rich texture associated with a good chole masala, many kitchens finish the dish with an extra tempering of ghee or a knob of butter, and sometimes more oil during the initial cooking. That alone can add 100–150 kcal per serving without adding any protein — a restaurant serving can run 220–280 kcal per 100g for the same 9g-protein chickpeas you'd get at home for far fewer calories.

sections.heading: Roasted chana: a snack, not a smaller bowl of chole
sections.body:
Dry roasted chana (roasted whole chickpeas, sold as a snack, or roasted chana dal known as putani/fried gram) is nutritionally different from boiled chana because it's dehydrated rather than cooked in water. Per 100g dry, roasted chana delivers approximately 19–20g protein and 360–380 kcal — roughly double the calorie density of boiled chole, gram for gram, because there's no water weight diluting it.

This makes roasted chana an efficient protein snack in small portions — a 25–30g handful gives about 5–6g protein at 100–115 kcal, comparable to a boiled egg. But it's easy to eat 100g without noticing, since it's dry and moreish, and that quietly becomes a 370-kcal snack. Portion it by weight, not by "a bowl," the way you would with any dense, dry food.

sections.heading: Fibre and blood sugar: chana's quiet strength
sections.body:
Chickpeas have a low-to-moderate glycaemic index (roughly 28–32), meaning they raise blood sugar slowly despite being carb-containing. This comes down to their fibre content and resistant starch, which slow digestion. At 7.6g fibre per 100g cooked, a single 150g serving of chole covers more than a third of a typical daily fibre target on its own.

This is one reason chole tends to be more satiating than an equivalent-calorie serving of plain rice or roti — the fibre slows gastric emptying and blunts the blood sugar spike that drives hunger an hour or two later.

sections.heading: Practical portioning: chole with rice or roti
sections.body:
Chickpeas, like most legumes, are missing one essential amino acid (methionine) in meaningful quantity but are rich in lysine — the reverse of grains like rice and wheat, which are low in lysine but carry methionine. Pairing chole with rice or roti isn't just tradition; it completes the amino acid profile, which is part of why chole chawal and chole bhature have persisted as combinations for generations.

For a practical target: a 200g serving of home-style chole (1–2 tsp oil) gives roughly 12–16g protein and 260–320 kcal. Add a cup of rice or two rotis, and you're looking at a complete-protein meal in the 450–550 kcal range — reasonable for lunch or dinner without needing bhature, which adds significant refined-flour and deep-fry calories on top.

key_takeaways: Plain boiled chickpeas: about 9g protein, 164 kcal, and 7.6g fibre per 100g cooked — one of the highest-fibre legumes in regular use
Chole's protein comes from the chana, not the gravy — but oil and butter in the gravy drive most of the calorie difference between home and restaurant versions
Restaurant chole can run nearly double the calories of home-cooked chole for the same chickpea content, mainly from added ghee or butter finishing
Roasted chana is calorie-dense (360–380 kcal per 100g dry) compared to boiled chole (164 kcal per 100g) — portion it like a snack, not a meal
Chickpeas' low glycaemic index and high fibre make chole genuinely filling; pairing with rice or roti completes the amino acid profile
